items.title: NHRC: Who will keep the keeper?
items.summary: On October 12, as the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) marked its 33rd Foundation Day. Its Chairperson, Justice V Ramasubramanian, described the office of the Chief Justice of India as one put to an agni pariksha (trial by fire) every minute, and “not necessarily by sacred souls”. Chief Justice Surya Kant offered a line that deserves to outlive the occasion: if the Constitution is the promise, the Commission is one of its keepers. It is a fine line. It also raises an uncomfortable question. Who ensures that the keeper is fit to keep? The question is not academic. Between November 9 and 20, the Sub-Committee on Accreditation of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) will decide whether the NHRC keeps the ‘A’ status it has held since 1999. In 2025, the Sub-Committee recommended a downgrade to ‘B’. The Commission’s challenge was rejected in December. Justice Amit Bansal passed the order on October 16 and set aside the trial court order of October 6, which had denied her permission. While passing the order, the Court said that a case under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA) will not act as a blanket bar on a person's right to travel abroad. “The fact that the petitioner has been charged of serious offences under the UAPA does not curtail her right to travel abroad in a blanket manner,” the High Court observed in its order. Therefore, the Court allowed her to travel on a personal bond of ₹1 lakh with her brother as surety. Justice Bansal further said she will not seek asylum in the UK or comment on the cases against her. items.summary: A Public Interest Litigation (PIL) has been filed before the Calcutta High Court seeking a uniform mandate for filing physical pleadings and documents in 75 GSM A4 paper in duplex (back-to-back) format in the High Court and other courts across West Bengal [Akash Sharma v. Registrar General, High Court at Calcutta and Another] . The PIL aims to lower paper consumption, printing services and costs and the physical bulk of court records. The case is listed for hearing on November 23. Calcutta High Court on February 22, 2021 had asked its administrative side to consider mandating use of A4 paper with double-side printing for pleadings and filings. However, the plea filed by advocate Akash Sharma states that further progress of the matter could not be ascertained through publicly available records or notices. This PIL primarily seeks to determine the outcome of the order dated February 22, 2021 and a fresh consideration of the matter to prescribe a uniform practice of using 75 GSM A4 paper in a duplex-printed format across all courts in the State.
